name: Melon de Bourgogne
say: muh-LOHN duh boor-GON-yuh, the wine moos-kah-DAY

lines.s10: Melon de Bourgogne makes Muscadet, the pale, bone dry, faintly salty white that the Loire pours with its oysters.
lines.s20: Melon de Bourgogne is the grape of Muscadet, grown where the Loire meets the Atlantic. It is light and bone dry, with green apple, lemon and a bready note from a winter resting on its yeast.
lines.s45: Melon de Bourgogne has one job, which is Muscadet, made where the Loire meets the Atlantic near Nantes. The grape itself is quiet: green apple, lemon and a little white peach. The wine is pale, light and bone dry, with brisk acidity and a salty finish. The cellar gives it its character. It rests through the winter on its lees, the spent yeast, which adds a bready note and sometimes a faint prickle. Pour it with oysters, mussels or fried fish. For all its name, it left Burgundy long ago, and it shares both its parents with Chardonnay.
lines.sale: Melon de Bourgogne, as Muscadet, is the oyster wine: light, salty and bone dry, with nothing to get in the way. I would pour it with the raw bar, or with anything fried and a squeeze of lemon.

glass.lead: Green apple, lemon and a little white peach, quiet and pale, with bread dough, oyster shell and a salty finish.

ladder.where: The Pays Nantais in most years, beside the Atlantic
The same vineyards in a warm, ripe year

glass.structure: Bone dry. Acidity high, alcohol low to moderate, body light; often a faint prickle of gas from bottling straight off the lees.

home.home: The Pays Nantais, where the Loire meets the Atlantic, above all Muscadet Sèvre et Maine. It is fermented cool with no new oak, and a wine labelled sur lie spends one winter on its lees and is bottled straight from them. The crus communaux, such as Clisson, Gorges and Le Pallet, stay on theirs about eighteen months to two years.
home.abroad: It rarely leaves home. In California it long passed for Pinot Blanc, until vine scientists put the name right, and a little is bottled under its own name in Oregon's Willamette Valley, in the same lean style.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius, cold from the ice bucket.
service.glass: A white wine glass, small enough to keep the wine cold.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; pour it cold and keep the bottle on ice.
service.age: Enjoy most bottles young; sur lie wines hold a few years, and the crus communaux keep far longer.

labels.means: The wine made from Melon de Bourgogne around Nantes; bone dry, and no relation of Muscat.
Kept one winter on its lees, the spent yeast, and bottled straight from them: more texture, a bready note.
The heart of Muscadet, named for two small rivers south east of Nantes.
Crus communaux: named villages whose wines rest on their lees for about eighteen months to two years.

guest.q: Is Muscadet the same as Muscat, and is it sweet?
guest.a: No, on both counts. Muscadet is made from Melon de Bourgogne and is bone dry, light and salty. Muscat is a different, perfumed grape that is often made sweet.

guest.q: What does sur lie on the label mean?
guest.a: The wine spent the winter on its lees, the spent yeast left after fermentation, and was bottled straight from them. That gives a rounder texture, a bready note and sometimes a faint prickle.

guest.q: Why is it called Melon of Burgundy if it comes from the Loire?
guest.a: It began in Burgundy, where it was once widely grown, and it has the same parents as Chardonnay. Today it is grown mostly around Nantes.

compare.tell: Chablis, which is Chardonnay, has more flesh and body, with chalk and green apple; Muscadet is lighter and saltier, with a bready note from its lees.
Albariño is salty too, but more aromatic, with white peach and apricot; Melon de Bourgogne is quieter, lighter and more bready.
Italian Pinot Grigio is as light and quiet, but lacks the bread dough and the salty finish that mark Melon de Bourgogne.

cards.front: Melon de Bourgogne: which wine does it make, and where?
cards.back: Muscadet, in the Pays Nantais, where the Loire meets the Atlantic near Nantes. Muscadet Sèvre et Maine is the heart of it.

cards.front: Melon de Bourgogne as Muscadet: what does sur lie on the label promise?
cards.back: One winter on the lees, the spent yeast, and bottling straight from them in the year after harvest: more texture, a bready note, sometimes a faint prickle.

cards.front: Melon de Bourgogne: who are its parents, and which grapes share them?
cards.back: Pinot and Gouais Blanc, the same pair that gave Chardonnay, Gamay and Aligoté. It began in Burgundy and found its home on the Loire.

questions.q: A blind white is water pale, light and bone dry, with green apple, lemon, bread dough and a salty finish, and a faint prickle on the tongue. Which wine is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: A quiet, light, salty white with bread dough and a faint prickle is Muscadet aged on its lees. Chablis has more flesh and chalk, and Albariño is more aromatic, with white peach.

questions.q: A guest sees Muscadet on the list and says she does not care for sweet Muscat. What do you tell her?

questions.exp: Muscadet is a bone dry Loire white made from Melon de Bourgogne. The name resembles Muscat, but the grape is a different one and the wine is not sweet.

questions.q: A guest wants a Muscadet with more depth, one that has rested on its lees for two years. Which names on the label do you look for?
questions.exp: Clisson and Gorges are crus communaux of Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, whose wines rest on their lees for about two years. Vouvray and Montlouis are Chenin Blanc, and Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it. The Codex's records on Melon de Bourgogne read true and nothing here departs from them.
Left out: the frost of 1709 as the reason the grape took over the Pays Nantais. This session's sources did not state it, though reference works do.
Left out: the number of crus communaux, which has grown since the first three of 2011 and may grow again.
The lees ageing of the crus is given as eighteen months or more, and about two years for Clisson and Gorges: the rule's own text gives 17 to 24 months at the least and the trade body 18 or 24.
The ladder's second rung is the same hills in a warm year: the grape has no true warm home.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after three fixes, one of them a fact the rule has changed.
changed: lines.s20 and the second question's explanation: Muscadet is no longer said to be made of one grape alone. The rule of the plain Muscadet appellation now admits Chardonnay as an accessory grape, at no more than 10 per cent of a holding's plantings; Sèvre et Maine, Coteaux de la Loire and Côtes de Grandlieu remain Melon alone.

worlds.home and the fourth label: the crus communaux rest on their lees about eighteen months to two years, in place of eighteen months or more. The rule's shortest term is a little under eighteen months and Clisson and Gorges ask two years.
glass.ladder, the second rung: the same vineyards, in place of the same hills.
open: The rule's own text for each cru could not be opened: the national institute's host lies outside this session's network. The trade press gives eighteen months, a retailer's notes two years, and the author read 17 to 24 months in the rule.

Two Codex records now say more than the rule does. The Loire reading in js/regions/france.json calls Melon Muscadet's only grape, and the Régionale question i-r0p7056l says it has been the sole grape of Muscadet ever since 1709. Both hold for the three named zones and no longer for the plain appellation.
